analysis.one_liner: Caps US greenhouse gas emissions by auctioning pollution permits and returns the revenue to households and public priorities.
analysis.headline: A climate bill with 92 Democratic cosponsors was sent to nine House committees and never received a committee vote or a floor vote before the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would set a national ceiling on greenhouse gas emissions that shrinks each year through 2050, requiring power plants and large industrial facilities to hold pollution permits. Most permits would be sold at auction, and the money would fund consumer rebates, deficit reduction, public transit, energy efficiency, and help for communities harmed by climate change. It would also charge importers of carbon-intensive goods, like steel and cement, the same pollution fee that US makers face, to keep factories from simply moving overseas.
analysis.who_benefits: Households, through a Climate Change Rebate Program funded by permit auction revenue, along with public transit riders, states that cut energy waste, and future generations facing less climate damage. US manufacturers of steel, cement, aluminum, and similar goods gain protection from imports made without carbon limits.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Households, transit riders, and US manufacturers

how_it_helps.text: Establishes a shrinking national cap on emissions from 2012 through 2050 and requires owners and operators of covered facilities to submit an allowance for each ton they emit.

Sells the emission allowances at auction and routes the revenue into a Citizen Protection Trust Fund and a Deficit Reduction Trust Fund, including a Climate Change Rebate Program and a healthy families fund.

Directs funds to public transportation grants, state energy-efficiency programs, natural resource adaptation, and aid for disadvantaged communities in trading-partner countries affected by climate change.

Requires importers of covered goods from countries without comparable climate programs to buy international reserve allowances, so foreign producers pay the same carbon cost as US facilities and domestic factories are not undercut.
Creates a Carbon Market Efficiency Board that can authorize cost relief if the permit market would pose substantial harm to the US economy.

analysis.who_pays: Owners of fossil fuel-fired power plants and energy-intensive manufacturers, who must hold or buy emission allowances (though the bill distributes some to them for free), and importers of carbon-intensive goods. Part of the cost would reach consumers through higher energy prices, partly offset by the rebate program.
analysis.who_pays_short: Fossil-fuel utilities, heavy industry, and importers

drawbacks.text: The bill creates a tradable permit market that any person may buy into, not just regulated facilities, which invites financial speculation in a market whose price is set by a shrinking supply.

Some allowances are distributed for free to fossil fuel power plants and energy-intensive manufacturers, which can let those firms profit from the program while their compliance costs are passed to customers; the bill also allows up to a quarter of compliance through domestic and international offsets, whose real-world integrity depends entirely on verification.

The border fee on carbon-intensive imports could raise prices on some consumer goods and risk friction with trading partners, which is why the bill directs the Secretary to adjust requirements to comply with US trade agreements.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill attacks a large, long-term public harm (climate change) while recycling most revenue back to households and public investment rather than into industry pockets, and it shields US factory jobs with border fees. Its main honest weaknesses are the free allowances that can create windfalls for utilities and heavy industry, the speculative trading market it opens, and the risk that offset credits and trade-agreement carve-outs dilute the emissions cap.

outcome.mechanism: It never got past committee referral — it was sent to nine House committees and then parked at subcommittees, and no chair ever scheduled a markup or a floor vote before Congress adjourned.

narrative.text: Rep. Lloyd Doggett introduced the Climate MATTERS Act on June 19, 2008, and 92 House Democrats signed on as cosponsors.
The House referred it to the Ways and Means Committee plus eight other committees, covering everything from tax and energy to agriculture and transportation.
Over the following five months, it was referred to four subcommittees on energy, highways, and conservation; the record shows no committee vote, no markup, and no floor action.
The bill expired when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009, without ever reaching a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil fuel utilities, energy-intensive manufacturers, and importers of carbon-intensive goods were better off because the bill died: they avoided a new obligation to pay for emissions and avoided border carbon fees. Ordinary households lost the rebate and clean-energy funding the bill promised, and continued to bear climate damage without a national program to address it.

for.name: Rep. Lloyd Doggett
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and designed it to route auction revenue to household rebates, deficit reduction, and transit while protecting US manufacturers with border fees.

against.name: House committee chairs (Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce)
against.role: Chairs of the primary committees of referral
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a markup; it sat at subcommittee after the nine-committee referral until Congress adjourned.

sides.party_line_note: All 92 cosponsors were House Democrats, including the sponsor; no Republican support appears in the record.

industries.note: They would face a shrinking cap and must hold allowances for every ton emitted, but the bill distributes some allowances to them for free, and compliance costs would be passed to consumers as higher power prices, partly offset by rebates.

industries.industry: Energy-intensive manufacturers (steel, cement, aluminum, chemicals, glass, pulp)
industries.note: They would owe allowances for their emissions but also receive free allowances and gain a border fee on carbon-intensive imports, protecting domestic plants from rivals without carbon limits.

industries.industry: Coal and other fossil fuel producers
industries.note: A falling national emissions cap shrinks demand for coal and other fossil fuels, which is the point of the program.
Importers of steel, cement, and similar goods from countries without comparable climate programs would have to buy international reserve allowances, raising the cost of those goods in the US market.

The bill creates a new multi-year market in emission allowances that is open to any holder, not just regulated facilities, giving financial firms a new asset class to trade; a Carbon Market Efficiency Board would police market cost shocks.
Auction revenue funds grants for transit construction, travel-demand projects, and state energy-efficiency programs, creating work and cheaper transportation options for the public.
